-U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright
campaigned for Texas Republican Senate candidate
Ken Paxton in Houston today.
From Houston Public Media, Natalie Weber reports
Wright announced new grants for power grid infrastructure.
-Sandwiched between an American flag and a Texas flag,
Wright announced more than $900 million in federal funding
to modernize the country's power grid.
As oil prices have skyrocketed during the U.S.
and Israel's war with Iran,
Wright touted the grant as an investment
that would lower consumers' energy costs.
And he took aim at his political opponents.
-Democrats have relentlessly pushed every policy possible

-Energy prices have become a flashpoint this election season,

NPR's Joel Rose reports today's announcement

after years of certification delays.
-The Federal Aviation Administration
says it has approved the largest version
of Boeing's best-selling 737 line
after extensive safety reviews
and thousands of hours of test flights.
-At one point, Boeing expected to begin delivering
the MAX 10 by 2023,
but the company faced a more stringent certification process
after two fatal crashes of the smaller MAX 8 model
in 2018 and 2019.
Boeing now expects to start delivering the MAX 10 next year
and says it has a lengthy backlog of orders
from airlines around the world.
The certification is the latest sign of growing confidence
in Boeing from U.S. regulators.
Joel Rose, NPR News, Washington.

A new study finds that people
with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
had a higher risk of dying from any cause,
but NPR's Maria Godoy reports taking ADHD medication
was linked to a lower risk of death.
-Researchers analyzed the findings of 19 studies
that included data from nearly 16 million people
with and without ADHD on three continents.
Some studies followed participants for more than 20 years.
They found that ADHD was linked to significantly higher risks
of suicide and injury deaths,
as well as a moderately higher risk
of dying from natural causes.
But they also found some evidence
that this risk of mortality
is lower among people who take ADHD medication.
The researchers say the findings underscore the need
for everyone who may have ADHD
to have access to accurate diagnoses and treatment.
The findings appear in the journal "JAMA Network Open."
Maria Godoy, NPR News.
